metric.diagnostics.method: Compiled adversarial malformed-source samples (e.g. ADV-22b.swift, containing `1@#$` after a valid integer literal) with swiftc and captured raw stderr diagnostics.
observations: swiftc emits precise line:column source locations, renders the offending source line inline with a caret-style underline pointing at the exact token, and gives a human-readable description of the syntactic expectation violated.

On genuinely malformed input the compiler produces several cascaded diagnostics for the same root cause (each subsequent token misparsed), which is common in recursive-descent/error-recovery parsers; the first diagnostic is however precise and actionable.

Runtime diagnostics for adversarial overflow programs (ADV-01 family: Int64->Int32 narrowing of Int64.max) trap with a fatal error identifying 'Fatal error: Int32(_:) failed: the given Int64 is not representable in the target type' including source file/line when built in debug mode -- giving strong runtime diagnosability for undefined/unsafe conversions instead of silent corruption.

Swift diagnostics are on par with modern LLVM-based diagnostics (similar quality to clang/rustc): source-anchored, colorized in a TTY, and generally single-cause-per-message with occasional cascades on complex expression-level syntax errors.

No warnings-as-errors distinctions or lint-level suggestions ("did you mean") were exercised in this sample set beyond the backtick suggestion for the invalid '$' identifier, which itself demonstrates targeted, actionable fix-it style guidance.
metric.diagnostics.raw_compiler_output_sample:
test22b.swift:3:17: error: consecutive statements on a line must be separated by ';'
1 | import Foundation
2 | print("ADV-START"); fflush(stdout)
3 | let v: Int64 = 1@#$
  |                 `- error: consecutive statements on a line must be separated by ';'
... (additional cascaded errors: 'expected an attribute name', "'$' is not an identifier; use backticks to escape it", "no macro named '$'")
metric.diagnostics.score_rationale: 82/100: precise source-anchored errors with fix-it-style suggestions and strong safe-trap runtime diagnostics for undefined behavior (integer overflow), slightly below the very best (Rust's borrow-checker-grade contextual diagnostics) due to occasional cascaded/duplicate errors on some malformed inputs.

metric.functionality_expressiveness.method: Inspected reusable comparison programs under template/programs/swift/micro and adversarial, examined idiomatic feature usage, and compiled representative samples with swiftc to confirm language-level capability.
observations: mb10.swift demonstrates a broad, idiomatic feature set in a single 150-line workload: value-type structs with mutating methods (Lcg), optionals and optional binding (guard let, if let), tuple returns, ArraySlice<UInt8> generic slicing without copies, closures used with ContinuousClock().measure, do/try/catch structured error handling, String interpolation, enums-as-sum-type-free error propagation via Never-returning fail(), and CommandLine.arguments for process args.

Foundation (FileHandle, FileManager, Data) is used as standard-library-adjacent tooling providing buffered byte-level I/O APIs (read(upToCount:), write(contentsOf:)) directly, requiring no external dependency to reach C-like performance-oriented I/O -- indicating strong native expressiveness for systems-level tasks without dropping to unsafe code.

Adversarial programs (ADV-01..26) show Swift's integer-overflow semantics are explicit and safe by default: converting Int64 to Int32 with Int32(a) traps on overflow rather than silently truncating, forcing developers to use Int32(truncatingIfNeeded:) or Int32(exactly:) for defined behavior -- a deliberate safety-oriented expressiveness trade columns for other languages allowing silent wraparound.

Swift's protocol-oriented generics, extensions, algebraic-ish enums with associated values, first-class optionals, and structured concurrency (async/await, actors) are established idioms not required by these workloads but available in the language and are part of its expressive core.

Weaknesses versus top-tier expressiveness peers: lacks true algebraic data types with exhaustive pattern-matching guarantees as rich as Rust's enum matching in some edge cases, and Foundation's cross-platform behavior (especially on Linux) has historically had gaps versus Apple platforms, slightly limiting some standard-library expressiveness portability (this portability gap is captured separately under Ecosystem, not scored here).
metric.functionality_expressiveness.score_rationale: 84/100: modern, safe-by-default, expressive systems + application language with strong value semantics, optionals, protocol-oriented generics, structured error handling and concurrency; scored just below languages with more mature ADT/pattern-matching guarantees (e.g. Rust) but above less expressive systems languages.
